value.body: A two-year master's in journalism and mass communication (often called MJMC or MA-JMC). It covers reporting, editing, media law and ethics, broadcast and digital production, advertising and public relations, and communication research. It suits graduates from any stream, including those who already hold a BJMC and want to specialise or teach.

items.label: Course length
items.note: 4 semesters; some institutes run one-year PG diplomas instead

value.title: How you get in
value.body: A bachelor's degree in any subject, usually with a minimum percentage set by the university. Central and many state universities admit through CUET-PG; others hold their own entrance test, written test plus interview, or admit on merit.

value.title: At a glance
items: Portfolio and internships count for a lot in media hiring — often as much as the degree itself.
Newsroom jobs are limited and entry pay is often low; many graduates move to digital content, PR, corporate communications or advertising.
UGC-NET in Mass Communication plus the master's is the route to assistant professor posts.
Fees vary widely between public universities and private media schools.

value.title: PG students in journalism & mass communication, by year
value.note: 'Journalism & Mass Communication Total' row at PG level; covers all PG programmes in the discipline, not only MJMC-labelled ones. AISHE counts only institutions that responded to the survey; coverage varies by year, so part of any change can reflect reporting rather than real growth.
